questions.prompt: Click one skeletal muscle fibre.
questions.hint: A long, striated, pink cylinder with flattened nuclei along its edge.
questions.explain: Each pink band is one fibre: a single multinucleated cell formed by the fusion of myoblasts, running the length of the fascicle. Its nuclei sit at the edge, under the sarcolemma, which distinguishes skeletal from cardiac and smooth muscle.

questions.prompt: Click a nucleus of a skeletal muscle fibre.
questions.hint: Small, dark, elongated, and at the very edge of a fibre.
questions.explain: Skeletal muscle nuclei are flattened and peripheral, pushed to the edge of the fibre by the myofibrils that fill it. A centrally placed nucleus in an adult fibre suggests regeneration or a myopathy.

questions.prompt: Zoom in until the cross-striations are clear, then click one sarcomere: the span from one A band to the next.
questions.hint: The outlined span at the centre of the view: one dark A band and one light I band across the middle fibre.
questions.explain: At high magnification the striations resolve into dark A bands (myosin) and light I bands (actin), and one sarcomere runs from Z line to Z line. It is the contractile unit; thousands in series make a myofibril shorten.

questions.prompt: A 22-year-old sprinter tears a hamstring. Which cell on this section will provide the new nuclei for the repaired fibres? Click it.
questions.hint: A small lens-shaped nucleus pressed against the outside of a fibre, not inside it.
questions.explain: Satellite cells are quiescent stem cells lying between the sarcolemma and the basal lamina of a fibre. After injury they divide, fuse with the damaged fibre or with each other, and supply new myonuclei; mature fibres cannot divide. On routine H&E a satellite cell cannot be told from a myonucleus with certainty (that takes a Pax7 or laminin stain); the cell accepted here is the flattened nucleus pressed onto the fibre surface in the centre of the view.

questions.prompt: Click the endomysium.
questions.hint: The pale strip between two fibres.
questions.explain: Endomysium is the thin reticular connective tissue sheath around each individual fibre, carrying the capillaries and nerve terminals. Perimysium wraps a fascicle and epimysium the whole muscle.

questions.prompt: Click the capillary.
questions.hint: A narrow tube with a red blood cell inside, lying between fibres.
questions.explain: Capillaries run in the endomysium parallel to the fibres, close enough that oxygen diffuses a few micrometres to the mitochondria. Endurance training raises the number of capillaries per fibre.

questions.prompt: Click one muscle fibre in cross-section.
questions.hint: A pink polygon with dark nuclei at its edge.
questions.explain: In cross-section each fibre is a polygon packed against its neighbours, with nuclei at the periphery. Fibre diameter is 10 to 100 micrometres; atrophy and hypertrophy are judged from this view.

questions.prompt: Click the perimysium.
questions.hint: The pale band surrounding a whole bundle of fibres.
questions.explain: Perimysium is the connective tissue that bundles fibres into a fascicle and carries the larger vessels and nerves into the muscle. Endomysium is finer and lies between individual fibres.

questions.prompt: A pathology resident must decide whether a biopsy is skeletal or cardiac muscle. Click the feature that tells them this is skeletal: a nucleus in its typical position.
questions.hint: Dark, flattened, right at the fibre's edge.
questions.explain: Skeletal muscle nuclei are peripheral, directly beneath the sarcolemma; cardiac myocytes have one or two central nuclei, intercalated discs and branching. Central nuclei in skeletal muscle mean regeneration or a myopathy such as myotonic dystrophy.

questions.prompt: Click one osteon (Haversian system).
questions.hint: A target of concentric rings with a hole in the middle.
questions.explain: An osteon is a cylinder of concentric lamellae around a central canal, the structural unit of compact bone. Osteocytes sit in lacunae between the lamellae and talk through canaliculi.

questions.prompt: Click a central (Haversian) canal.
questions.hint: The empty circle at the centre of the rings.
questions.explain: The central canal runs along the axis of the osteon and carries a capillary, a venule and a nerve fibre. Volkmann (perforating) canals connect neighbouring central canals and the periosteal vessels at right angles.

questions.prompt: Click an osteocyte lacuna.
questions.hint: A small dark lens between the lamellae, with fine lines (canaliculi) radiating from it.
questions.explain: Osteocytes are osteoblasts that became trapped in the matrix they secreted. Each occupies a lens-shaped lacuna and extends processes through canaliculi to its neighbours and to the canal, sensing load and regulating remodelling. This is a ground section, so the cells themselves are gone: what you see are the empty lacunae and canaliculi, made dark by trapped debris and air.

questions.prompt: A 70-year-old with Paget disease of bone has very high alkaline phosphatase and bone pain. The biopsy is described as a 'mosaic'. Click the kind of line that builds that mosaic.
questions.hint: A thin bright line around the outer edge of an osteon, where its lamellae stop.
questions.explain: Cement (reversal) lines mark where osteoclasts stopped resorbing bone and osteoblasts started laying down a new osteon. In Paget disease overactive osteoclasts and chaotic rebuilding leave so many irregular cement lines that the bone looks like a jigsaw, the mosaic pattern. Bisphosphonates work by switching the osteoclasts off.

questions.prompt: Click the myelin sheath of one axon.
questions.hint: The pale ring around a central dot.
questions.explain: In a transverse section a myelinated axon is a small dark dot inside a pale ring; the ring is the myelin, lipid-rich lamellae laid down by one Schwann cell per internode. Most of the lipid is lost in routine H&E processing, so the ring looks empty.

questions.prompt: Click an axon.
questions.hint: The small dark centre, not the ring around it.
questions.explain: The axon is the central dot inside the myelin ring. Axon diameter and myelin thickness set conduction velocity: large myelinated motor fibres conduct at up to 120 m/s, small unmyelinated pain fibres at about 1 m/s.

questions.prompt: A toxin injected next to a nerve fails to reach the axons because of a barrier layer. Click that layer.
questions.hint: The band that wraps one bundle of axons.
questions.explain: The perineurium is a sleeve of flattened epithelioid cells joined by tight junctions around each fascicle; it forms the blood-nerve barrier. Epineurium is the loose outer coat of the whole nerve and endoneurium the fine tissue between axons.

questions.prompt: A patient with Guillain-Barré syndrome has an immune attack on the cells that make peripheral myelin. Click the nucleus of one such cell.
questions.hint: A crescent-shaped dark nucleus hugging the outside of a myelin ring.
questions.explain: Schwann cells myelinate peripheral axons, one cell per internode, and their crescent-shaped nuclei lie against the myelin ring. In Guillain-Barré syndrome antibodies strip the myelin, slowing conduction and causing ascending weakness.

questions.prompt: Click the nucleus of an endothelial cell.
questions.hint: A flat dark nucleus right at the edge of the lumen.
questions.explain: Endothelial cells form the single flattened layer lining the lumen; their nuclei bulge slightly into it. They are the tunica intima's working surface: they control clotting, vessel tone and leukocyte entry.

questions.prompt: Click the nucleus of a smooth muscle cell in the tunica media.
questions.hint: One of the many elongated nuclei in the thick middle ring.
questions.explain: The media of a muscular artery is layer upon layer of circumferential smooth muscle cells whose elongated nuclei run around the vessel. Their tone, set by sympathetic nerves and local factors, controls blood flow to the limb.

questions.prompt: Click the internal elastic lamina.
questions.hint: The bright wavy line just outside the endothelium.
questions.explain: The internal elastic lamina is a fenestrated sheet of elastin between the intima and the media, wavy because the vessel contracted at death. Its presence and prominence are a marker of a muscular artery; veins have a thin or absent one.

questions.prompt: An aneurysm repair surgeon notes that the outer coat of the artery carries its own tiny nutrient vessels. Click that coat.
questions.hint: The outermost pale, wavy layer.
questions.explain: The tunica adventitia is loose collagenous tissue with fibroblasts, nerves and the vasa vasorum that feed the outer media of large vessels. In an aortic dissection, blood tracks between media layers and may rupture through the adventitia.
